habitat: Pairs in mixed bushveld and woodland, always in drier country than Cape Batis. It feeds in the mid- and lower strata and often joins bird parties.
summary: A very common resident. A small pied bird with a grey cap and yellow eyes. The male lacks any rufous. The female has a clearly defined rich rufous chin-spot and breast-band, and white flanks. The most characteristic call is a descending choi-choi-choi, like three blind mice. It also calls chi-chirr or chee-chir-chir, and it is one of the first birds heard at dawn. Bill, leg and wing colours were not described. The Kemp paper name Chinspot Batis and the code RB were left unchanged.

similar.note: Cape Batis lives in moister forest. Its male has rufous flanks and both sexes have rufous wing coverts. Chinspot Batis is the dry-country bird, and its male lacks rufous.

research.note: Newman calls it a very common resident, and Avibase does not mark the Kruger occurrence rare or accidental, so status is resident and all twelve months are listed. The male breast colour is not named. Newman only says he lacks rufous, and the family notes describe black or rufous breast-bands, which is why this needs review. The immature is only the family note that it is a dull version of the adult. Bill, legs and wings were not given colours. No flight photograph was found. The grade A call is from Kruger near Skukuza. Its filename includes Unid2 and a 250 Hz high-pass, and this site has not filtered it further. Population figures, the Kemp paper name Chinspot Batis and the code RB were left unchanged.
